draft.title: Strict liability offences
card: Most crimes need the prosecution to prove a guilty act and a guilty mind, which means intent or knowledge.
A strict liability offence is different. The prosecution need only prove the act happened. It does not have to prove intent.
Many traffic offences work this way, such as driving over the speed limit. It does not matter if the driver did not mean to speed.
The accused may still raise a defence, such as an honest and reasonable mistake of fact, but the prosecution does not need to prove a guilty mind.
draft.remember: Strict liability: prove the act, not the intent.

a.q: Sam is fined for driving 15 km/h over the limit in Mildura. He says he did not notice his speed. Why is this not a good reason to avoid the offence?
opts: Speeding is strict liability, so intent need not be proven
Speeding needs proof that the driver meant to speed
Speeding is only an offence if someone is hurt
A driver who did not notice cannot be charged
a.why: For strict liability offences the prosecution only needs to prove the act. Sam not noticing means he lacked intent, but intent is not required to be proven.
a.clue: What must the prosecution prove for this kind of offence?

b.q: Which feature makes an offence strict liability?
opts: The prosecution does not have to prove the accused's intent
The accused must prove they had no intent
The penalty is always a fine rather than prison
The act must have caused serious harm
b.why: What marks a strict liability offence is that only the act needs to be proven. The accused does not carry a burden to prove lack of intent, and the penalty or harm is not what defines it.
b.clue: Focus on what the prosecution can leave out.

a.best: Speeding is strict liability, so intent need not be proven
